passage:
Day one: at the Bhopal railway station, four-year-old Eshaan stood still and stared at a man with a large white beard, following him with his eyes. His father Mridul noticed the man glance back uneasily. "Come here, Eshaan." Mridul crouched. "You're curious. But people can feel uncomfortable when we look for a long time."
Day three: Eshaan noticed a woman with a bright tattoo, opened his mouth, and then looked at his dad instead.
Day six: he whispered, "Papa, can I say hello?" and waved.

qa.q: Where was Eshaan when he first stared at the man?
qa.a: He was at the Bhopal railway station.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he stared at the bearded man, and what might the man have felt?
qa.a: Eshaan was curious, since he simply followed the man with his eyes. The man might have felt uncomfortable, as he glanced back uneasily.

qa.q: What made Mridul's approach helpful?
qa.a: He crouched, named Eshaan's curiosity and calmly explained that staring can make people uncomfortable, without shaming him.

qa.q: How might the man with the white beard have felt on day six if Eshaan waved?
qa.a: He might have felt relieved and welcomed, since a wave and hello feel friendlier than a long stare.

grounding: A child stares from curiosity and learns, through kind explanation, that staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage: The monsoon had flooded the bus stop, and Avni, five, stood under the shelter with her aunt Kashish, both crowded against strangers. Avni stared at a girl in a wheelchair, turning her head as the girl rolled past. Kashish felt heat in her face. She bent down and whispered, "You're wondering about her wheels, aren't you? It's okay to be curious. It's better to ask than to stare. Let's smile and say hello if she wants to talk." Avni smiled, and the girl smiled back.

qa.q: Where were Avni and Kashish standing?
qa.a: They were standing under the shelter at a flooded bus stop.

qa.q: What was Avni probably thinking about as she stared at the girl?
qa.a: She was probably curious about the wheels, which is what Kashish guessed. She could also have been simply fascinated by something new.

qa.q: What did Kashish do well when she saw Avni staring?
qa.a: She stayed kind and said it was okay to be curious, then gave Avni a friendly alternative instead of shaming her.

qa.q: How might the girl in the wheelchair feel about being stared at, and about the smile?
qa.a: A long stare may feel uncomfortable, whereas a smile can make her feel included and respected.

grounding: A child's curious staring can be redirected by kind explanation instead of shame.

passage: In the busy Lajpat market lane, Vasudha stopped holding the bag and stared. A woman in a wheelchair was buying bangles, and Vasudha's eyes followed the wheels as they turned. She kept staring even as her mother, Vandana, walked on. Vandana came back and knelt. “You're curious about the wheelchair, na? It helps her move, like our legs help us.” Vasudha nodded, still looking. “When we stare for a long time, people can feel uncomfortable. Can you smile and say hello instead?” Vasudha smiled at the woman, who waved.

qa.q: What was the woman in the wheelchair buying?
qa.a: Bangles.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha keep staring at the wheels?
qa.a: She was curious and interested in how the wheelchair worked. She may also have felt unsure, because she had not seen one up close before.

qa.q: What did Vandana do instead of scolding?
qa.a: She explained kindly what the wheelchair does, said long staring can make people uncomfortable, and suggested smiling and saying hello instead.

qa.q: How might the woman see a child who stares versus one who smiles?
qa.a: A long stare may make her feel watched or different, while a smile and hello treats her like any other shopper.

grounding: A child stares at an unusual sight from curiosity, and her mother kindly explains that staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage:
“Mashi, look! His face has pictures on it!”
Bidisha glanced at the bus stop. A young man had a tattoo of vines along his jaw. Sachin was staring, mouth open.
“It's called a tattoo, Sachin. Lots of people choose them.”
“Does it hurt? Why is it on his face?”
“Good questions. But he can see you staring, and that might feel strange for him.”
Sachin looked at his feet. “Am I bad?”
“No, sona. You're curious. Let's wonder quietly and ask me at home.”
Sachin nodded and gave the man a small wave.

qa.q: What was on the young man's face?
qa.a: A tattoo of vines along his jaw.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he asked, “Am I bad?”
qa.a: He likely felt worried and a bit ashamed that staring was wrong. Before that, he was curious and excited about the tattoo.

qa.q: How did Bidisha support Sachin's curiosity?
qa.a: She named the tattoo, praised his questions, and suggested saving them for home instead of shaming him.

qa.q: If you were the young man, what would you want?
qa.a: You would probably want to be treated normally, perhaps with a smile or a wave, rather than a long, open-mouthed stare.

grounding: A child stares at an unfamiliar person from curiosity, and his aunt kindly explains why staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage:
Daycare note, written by Rukmini (childminder).
Today Aarti's grandmother came to pick her up. She has a large burn scar on one cheek. Bhupen stared at her all through shoe time, and even followed her to the gate with his eyes. She noticed and looked away. Later, I sat with Bhupen and told him, “You were wondering about her cheek. It's a scar from an old burn, and it doesn't hurt now. Staring can make people feel sad.” He asked if he could say bye to her tomorrow. I said yes.

qa.q: What did Bhupen follow with his eyes?
qa.a: Aarti's grandmother, all the way to the gate.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been thinking while he stared?
qa.a: He was probably curious and puzzled about the scar, wondering what happened. He may also have felt a little worried about whether it hurt.

qa.q: What would you advise Rukmini to do tomorrow when the grandmother comes?
qa.a: Stay close while Bhupen says bye, so it becomes a friendly moment, and praise him quietly for greeting her kindly.

qa.q: What is it like for the grandmother when a child stares at her cheek?
qa.a: She may feel noticed for her scar rather than as a person, which is why she looked away.

grounding: The note shows a child staring from curiosity and a childminder explaining kindly, without shaming, that staring can make others uncomfortable.

passage:
The temple fair in the village was crowded, but Tanuja only had eyes for one person: a visitor with bright blue hair and a big camera. Tanuja stared, mouth open, and trailed after her from the bangle stall to the swings.

The visitor turned, caught Tanuja staring again, and shifted her camera bag, looking unsure.

Jahnavi Didi crouched beside her sister. "Blue hair is new for you, na? But when someone keeps staring, it can feel odd. Try smiling and saying namaste."

Tanuja smiled. The visitor smiled back.

qa.q: What colour was the visitor's hair?
qa.a: Bright blue.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja keep staring and following the visitor?
qa.a: She was most likely curious and fascinated by the blue hair, something she had never seen. She may also have been drawn to the big camera.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi Didi handle the staring?
qa.a: She explained kindly why staring can feel odd and gave Tanuja something friendly to do instead, without shaming her.

qa.q: How does the visitor feel when Tanuja keeps staring?
qa.a: The visitor seems uneasy, shifting the camera bag and looking unsure, until Tanuja's smile turns it into a friendly moment.

grounding: It shows a young child staring at an unusual sight out of curiosity and an older sister kindly explaining how staring can feel to others.
